\chapter{Welcoming a Guest}
\label{ch:ml-welcoming-a-guest}
\hlchaptermodality{52}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the five things a guest meets at a Kerala doorway in Malayalam.}

Complete ML-C52-garland and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vātil]{\ml{വാതിൽ} (vātil) — a door}

\label{lesson:ML-C52-door}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{anugrahaṁ} mean, and what did \emph{vandanaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വാതിൽ}}
\textbf{\ml{വാതിൽ}} (\emph{vātil}) — \textquotedblleft{}a door\textquotedblright{}.

Tamil writes its door-word \ta{வாயில்} (\emph{vāyil}), and once you see it beside \ta{வாய்} — the mouth this book has already taught — the picture is hard to unsee. A doorway is the mouth of a house.

Malayalam's \ml{വാതിൽ} is the same word with a \emph{t} where Tamil has a \emph{y}, and the dictionaries connect the two. The mouth-word itself, \ml{വായ്}, sits in this book's chapter on the face.

Kannada says \ka{ಬಾಗಿಲು} (\emph{bāgilu}), which is a different word altogether. The chillu \ml{ൽ} at the end here is the same one that closed the leg-word and the finger-word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things a guest meets at the door.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vātil}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vātil}, then \emph{vāy}, and hear what a doorway is named for
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വാതിൽ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a door\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kasēra]{\ml{കസേര} (kasēra) — a chair}

\label{lesson:ML-C52-chair}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vātil} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കസേര}}
\textbf{\ml{കസേര}} (\emph{kasēra}) — \textquotedblleft{}a chair\textquotedblright{}.

Portuguese \emph{cadeira}, come ashore on the Malabar coast and settled. Kerala's Portuguese layer is thick and domestic: the table, the cupboard and the window in an ordinary Malayalam room are all Portuguese words worn into Malayalam shapes — \ml{മേശ} (\emph{mēśa}), \ml{അലമാര} (\emph{alamāra}), \ml{ജനൽ} (\emph{janal}).

Furniture travels with the people who make it, and the vocabulary of a room records who was in it. This is one of the few places in this book where the trail is only five centuries long instead of five thousand.

Kannada's \ka{ಕುರ್ಚಿ} (\emph{kurci}) is a chair too, and it arrived from the north along an entirely different road.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: a door, and a chair.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kasēra}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kasēra}, then \emph{vātil}, the way in and the seat beyond it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{കസേര} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a chair\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kōlaṁ]{\ml{കോലം} (kōlaṁ) — the pattern drawn at a doorway}

\label{lesson:ML-C52-kolam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kasēra} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കോലം}}
\textbf{\ml{കോലം}} (\emph{kōlaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}the pattern drawn at a doorway\textquotedblright{}.

Native Dravidian, and its plain sense is 'form, shape, guise'. The pattern chalked on the ground at a threshold is a shape laid down, and Tamil uses \ta{கோலம்} for the same thing.

The word keeps its wider life alongside the drawing: a person in costume, an animal's markings, anything that has taken on a form, can be a \ml{കോലം}.

Kannada names the same threshold drawing \ka{ರಂಗೋಲಿ} (\emph{raṅgōli}), a word built on Sanskrit colour. One sister named the practice for its shape and the other for its pigment.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three. A door, a chair, the pattern at the threshold.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kōlaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kōlaṁ}, then \emph{vātil}, and put the drawing back where it is drawn
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{കോലം} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the pattern drawn at a doorway\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pūvŭ]{\ml{പൂവ്} (pūvŭ) — a flower}

\label{lesson:ML-C52-flower}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kōlaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{പൂവ്}}
\textbf{\ml{പൂവ്}} (\emph{pūvŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{}.

Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*pū}, one of the shortest words the family has and one of the best kept: Tamil \ta{பூ}, Telugu \te{పువ్వు}, Kannada \ka{ಹೂವು}. Kannada's \emph{h} is that opening shift again, met first at the fruit.

Kerala puts the word to work at the front of a compound: the flower-carpet laid out for the harvest festival is \ml{പൂക്കളം}, the flower plus a word for a laid-out ground.

Malayalam's own form adds a \emph{v} and the half-vowel, which is why it looks longer than Tamil's bare two letters while saying the same thing.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four. A door, a chair, the pattern at the threshold, a flower.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pūvŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{pūvŭ}, then \emph{kōlaṁ}, the two things laid at a doorway
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{പൂവ്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[māla]{\ml{മാല} (māla) — a garland}

\label{lesson:ML-C52-garland}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pūvŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മാല}}
\textbf{\ml{മാല}} (\emph{māla}) — \textquotedblleft{}a garland\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{mālā}, a garland or a string of things, borrowed all across the south. Kannada's \ka{ಹೂಮಾಲೆ} (\emph{hūmāle}) is this word with the flower-word stuck on the front of it, so the Kannada compound spells out what Malayalam leaves to context.

The word is also a string in the abstract — a series, a row — which is why a rosary and a necklace and a list can all be one.

And that closes the door: the way in, the seat, the pattern on the ground, the flower and the garland. A guest arriving at a Kerala house in the old way would meet all five before a word was exchanged.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: a door, a chair, the pattern at the threshold, a flower, a garland.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{māla}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{vātil}, \emph{kasēra}, \emph{kōlaṁ}, \emph{pūvŭ}, \emph{māla}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{മാല} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a garland\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
